opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of testing against known, public jailbreaks as a baseline hygiene check more than a real measure of robustness. These techniques are out there: role-play framings, "grandma" prompts, encoding tricks, many-shot attacks, the classic DAN-style templates. Anyone with a search engine can find them. So if a frontier model still falls to something that's been circulating on Reddit for a year, that's a sign the developer isn't doing basic due diligence. It's the equivalent of shipping software with a vulnerability that already has a public CVE.

But I'd caution against reading too much into passing those tests. Known jailbreaks are, almost by definition, the ones developers have had the chance to patch. Often the model has effectively been trained against that exact distribution, so you're measuring whether the model memorized the defense, not whether it's robust in a deeper sense. In our research we've repeatedly seen that small perturbations, or a fresh attack from an automated red-teaming method, get through defenses that look solid against the public benchmark set. There's a real gap between "robust to yesterday's attacks" and "robust to a motivated adversary."

So I see it as necessary but not sufficient. It sets a floor and catches regressions, which matters, since a new fine-tune can quietly undo safety training. It also gives a common yardstick for comparing models. But if we want to know whether a model is safe to deploy with genuinely dangerous capabilities, we need adaptive evaluation: red-teamers with real budgets, automated attack search, white-box or fine-tuning access where that's the realistic threat model. The question to ask isn't "does it resist the attacks we know about?" but "how much effort does it take for a capable attacker to break it, and is that cost high enough given what's at stake?"

r001.rationale: The response frames public jailbreak tests as a baseline check that catches models still vulnerable to known attacks and regressions in their defenses.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that it's a floor, not a ceiling. If a model falls to a jailbreak that's been circulating on Twitter or in a published paper for six months, that tells you something pretty damning about the robustness of the safety training. These are the attacks the developer had every opportunity to see coming. So the main point of testing against known techniques is to catch failures that there's really no excuse for, and to establish a baseline that lets you compare across models and across versions of the same model in a reasonably apples-to-apples way.

The second thing is that known techniques tend to be representative of attack families, not just individual strings. A specific prompt might get patched, but the underlying mechanism, say, persona role-play, or encoding the harmful request in a different format, or many-shot in-context priming, those mechanisms are what you actually care about. So when we run public jailbreaks, we're often less interested in whether that exact prompt works and more interested in whether small variations on it work. If a model is robust to the canonical version but breaks the moment you paraphrase it or translate it or change the framing slightly, then the defense is probably pattern-matching on surface features rather than actually understanding the intent, and that's not going to hold up against a motivated adversary.

Where I'd push back on over-relying on it is that the threat model you actually care about, especially as these systems become more capable, is a sophisticated attacker with real resources and time, not a hobbyist copying things off a forum. Those attackers are going to develop novel techniques. So public jailbreaks are a necessary but very much not sufficient test. If you pass, you've cleared a low bar. If you fail, you've got a serious problem. And I think the honest picture right now is that most frontier models still fail some meaningful fraction of these, which is sobering given how long this has been an active area.

The last thing I'd mention is that there's real value in the transparency aspect. Because the techniques are public, external researchers like us can run them, developers can't really dispute the results, and you get something like an independent audit. That's harder to achieve with proprietary red-teaming, where you're largely taking the lab's word for it about what they tested and how.

r001.rationale: The response says testing public jailbreaks catches failures against known attacks and checks whether models withstand canonical techniques and their variations.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a basic sanity check. If there’s a jailbreak that’s publicly available, that anyone can find and try, then it’s reasonable to expect a model to be robust to it. Testing those attacks tells you whether the defenses are keeping up with threats we already know about.

But there’s an important asymmetry: failing that test is strong evidence of a vulnerability, while passing it is fairly weak evidence of safety. The model might have been trained specifically to resist those techniques, without addressing the underlying problem. A new attack, or even a variation on an existing one, could still work.

So these tests are useful as a baseline, but we also need adaptive testing—where someone actively tries to find a way around the defenses of the particular model we’re evaluating.

r001.rationale: The response says testing publicly available jailbreaks checks whether the model is robust to them and whether its defenses address known threats.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a basic sanity check. If a jailbreak is already public, we should assume that someone who wants to misuse the model can find it and try it. So testing against those attacks tells us whether the model is vulnerable to threats we already know about.

But there’s a real asymmetry here: failing that test is informative; passing it gives you much less assurance. The model may have been trained specifically to resist those examples without becoming robust to the underlying attack. So it’s a useful baseline, but you also need people actively looking for new attacks, rather than treating a fixed set of public jailbreaks as a comprehensive safety assessment.

r001.rationale: The response says testing public jailbreak attacks shows whether the model is vulnerable to known threats, which communicates checking whether those techniques are defended against.
